NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- Three weeks after an apparent misunderstanding sparked a confrontation, deadly Hindu-Christian riots continue unabated in the remote east Indian state of Orissa. Police officers chase away a protester in Mangalore, India, Monday. By Tuesday, about 20 deaths had been reported, said Praveen Kumar, the superintendent of police in the worst-affected Kandhamal district. The latest casualty is a police officer who died after an armed mob of about 400 to 500 mostly Hindus torched a police station in the district on Monday, Orissa state police said. Orissa's Director General of Police G.C. Nanda the policeman died when the mob opened fire at officers fleeing the burning building. The violence spread to southern India over the weekend when vandals attacked 14 churches in an hour in the state of Karnataka Sunday, the network said. The Christian community in the Karnataka -- numbering about 2.5 million -- said right-wing Hindus are targeting them for opposing the violence in Orissa. By Tuesday, police had arrested about 140 people in connection with the riots, said Karnataka's Inspector General of Police A.M. Prasad. Sixty of them -- all Hindus -- were arrested for the church attacks, Prasad said. The rest, mostly Christians, were charged with disturbing the peace, he said. Orissa has historically been a tinderbox of Hindu-Christian tensions. Some Hindu groups view the work of Christian missionaries in the state with suspicion. They accuse missionaries of bribing or forcing Hindus into converting. The seeds for the current conflict were planted on August 23, when Hindu leader, Laxmananda Saraswati, and four others were killed in Kandhamal after 20 to 30 gunmen barged into a Hindu school and began shooting, the Orissa chief minister's office said. The authorities have not determined who killed Saraswati, but after the incident they detained five people who are Christians, said Sukanta Panda, spokesman for the chief minister. The government says the killings may have been the work of Maoist rebels -- investigators have many unanswered questions -- but some hardline Hindus blamed a Christian minority. They took to the streets in anger, rampaging through predominantly Christian neighborhoods, ransacking shops and torching houses. They chopped down trees to block roads, making it difficult for police to reach trouble spots. A Christian orphanage was set on fire. A 20-year-old woman, who was teaching children inside, burned to death. Christian residents fought back, and the clashes spread. Authorities imposed a night curfew in many towns and deployed state and federal forces in the troubled areas, Kumar -- the police superintendent -- said. Both sides said the violence has left Christian churches and Hindu temples razed to the ground. This is not the first time the simmering anger has boiled over in the state with deadly consequences. In 1999, a Hindu mob burned to death an Australian missionary, Graham Staines, and his two children while they slept inside their car. And last Christmas, clashing groups killed four people and burned several churches in the same Orissa district -- Kandhamal. Maoist rebels, who claim to be fighting for the poor and the dispossessed, have been battling the Indian government in an insurgency that has resulted in thousands of casualties since the late 1960s. Some Christians accept the Maoist theory, saying the rebels have also struck against hard-line Hindus because they associate them as being closely aligned with the government. But Hindu groups insists that Christians were behind Saraswati's death. Unlike Orissa, Karnataka has until now been spared the large-scale clash between Christians and Hindus. But now, many in the Christian community fear their calm and prosperous state may become another battleground between the two religions, CNN-IBN said. CNN's Harmeet Singh contributed to this report .

The most recent death was that of a police officer, Orissa state police said. Nanda, said the officer died when the mob fired at police personnel as they escaped from the burning station. Nanda said the assault may have been revenge for arrests made by police during the continuing sectarian violence.

The attack occurred two days after police opened fire on a crowd to stop it from assaulting Christian residents. CNN’s sister network, CNN-IBN, reported that between three and six people were killed in that shooting.

Over the weekend, the unrest reached southern India. CNN-IBN said vandals attacked 14 churches within one hour on Sunday in Karnataka state. Karnataka’s Christian population, estimated at about 2.5 million, said right-wing Hindus were targeting them because they had spoken out against the violence in Orissa.

By Tuesday, police had detained around 140 people in relation to the riots, said A.M. Prasad, Karnataka’s inspector general of police. Prasad said 60 of those arrested — all Hindus — were held over the attacks on churches. The remaining detainees, most of them Christians, were accused of breaching the peace.

Orissa has long been a flashpoint for tensions between Hindus and Christians. Some Hindu organizations distrust Christian missionary activity in the state, accusing missionaries of using money or coercion to convert Hindus.

The current wave of violence began after events on August 23, when Hindu leader Laxmananda Saraswati and four other people were killed in Kandhamal. According to the office of Orissa’s chief minister, 20 to 30 armed men entered a Hindu school and opened fire. Authorities have not identified those responsible for Saraswati’s killing, but five Christians were detained afterward, said Sukanta Panda, a spokesman for the chief minister.

The government has said Maoist rebels may have carried out the killings, though investigators still have many unresolved questions. However, some hard-line Hindus blamed the Christian minority. Angry groups then moved through largely Christian neighborhoods, looting stores and setting homes ablaze. They also cut down trees to block roads, hampering police efforts to reach affected areas.

A Christian orphanage was burned down. A 20-year-old woman who had been teaching children inside died in the fire.

Christian residents retaliated, and the fighting widened. Authorities placed many towns under nighttime curfews and sent both state and federal security forces into the disturbed areas, police superintendent Kumar said.

Both communities said the violence has resulted in Christian churches and Hindu temples being destroyed.

This is not the first time long-standing hostility in Orissa has erupted with deadly results. In 1999, a Hindu mob burned Australian missionary Graham Staines and his two children to death while they were sleeping in their car. Last Christmas, rival groups killed four people and set several churches on fire in Kandhamal, the same district now at the center of the unrest.

Maoist rebels, who say they are fighting on behalf of the poor and dispossessed, have waged an insurgency against the Indian government since the late 1960s, causing thousands of casualties. Some Christians believe the theory that Maoists killed Saraswati, arguing that the rebels have also attacked hard-line Hindus because they view them as closely linked to the government.

Hindu groups, however, continue to insist that Christians were responsible for Saraswati’s death.

Unlike Orissa, Karnataka had previously avoided large-scale violence between Hindus and Christians. But CNN-IBN reported that many Christians there now worry their peaceful and economically successful state could become another arena of conflict between the two faiths.

Maoist rebels reportedly claimed responsibility for the killing, but Hindu nationalist groups blamed local Christians, an accusation Christian leaders strongly denied. The killing quickly sparked retaliatory attacks against Christian communities in Orissa.

The unrest has also raised alarm beyond Orissa. In the southern state of Karnataka, churches and Christian prayer halls were attacked in several cities and towns, including Mangalore and Bangalore. Karnataka officials defended the police response, saying security forces were deployed to protect churches and restore order. However, images of police clashing with Christian protesters outside damaged churches intensified criticism from rights groups and opposition politicians.

India’s central government has urged state authorities to protect minorities and maintain law and order. Christian organizations have called for an independent investigation into the violence, compensation for victims and prosecution of those responsible for attacks on churches and homes.

The violence in Orissa highlights long-running tensions in parts of India where religion, caste, tribal identity and politics intersect. Hindu nationalist groups have accused Christian missionaries of converting poor tribal and lower-caste Hindus through inducements, while Christian leaders say conversions are voluntary and that minority communities are being targeted for their faith.

For displaced families in Kandhamal, the immediate concern remains survival. Many say they are afraid to return home, fearing renewed attacks if security forces withdraw.

# Violence in India’s Orissa State Leaves Dozens Dead, Churches Attacked

**BHUBANESWAR, India** — Communal violence in India’s eastern state of Orissa in 2008 left dozens of people dead, thousands displaced and scores of churches and Christian institutions damaged or destroyed, after the killing of a prominent Hindu religious leader triggered weeks of unrest.

The violence, centered largely in Kandhamal district, erupted after **Swami Laxmanananda Saraswati**, a Hindu nationalist leader associated with the Vishwa Hindu Parishad, was shot dead along with several associates on **August 23, 2008**. Although Maoist rebels later claimed responsibility for the killing, Hindu nationalist groups accused local Christians of involvement, a claim Christian leaders denied.

Police officials at the time said the killing sparked retaliatory attacks across remote villages in Kandhamal, where long-standing tensions between Hindu and Christian communities had been simmering for years.

## Death Toll and Displacement

Official figures placed the death toll at around **38 to 40 people**, though Christian organizations and human rights groups have said the number may have been significantly higher, with some estimates exceeding **90 deaths**. Thousands of homes were burned, and tens of thousands of people fled to forests, relief camps or neighboring districts.

State officials said more than **20,000 people** were housed in government-run relief camps at the height of the violence. Rights groups estimated that as many as **50,000 people** may have been displaced.

Police officials in Orissa said security forces were deployed to the worst-hit areas, but the geography of Kandhamal — a hilly, forested district with scattered villages — made it difficult to contain mobs quickly.

## Churches and Christian Institutions Targeted

Christian groups reported widespread attacks on churches, prayer halls, convents, schools and charitable institutions. Estimates varied, but rights organizations said **hundreds of churches and Christian places of worship** were damaged or destroyed during the violence.

Homes belonging to Christians were burned in village after village, according to survivors and aid workers. Some victims said they were forced to renounce Christianity or flee. Hindu organizations denied that the violence was centrally organized, describing it instead as anger over the killing of Saraswati.

Police officials said they received reports of arson, looting and assaults across multiple blocks of Kandhamal district. Officers also said that several cases were registered in connection with mob attacks, killings and destruction of property.

## Roots of Hindu-Christian Tensions

The riots exposed deep religious and social tensions in the region. Kandhamal has a significant Christian population, many of them from marginalized tribal and Dalit communities. Hindu nationalist groups had long accused Christian missionaries of using inducements to convert poor villagers, a charge church leaders rejected.

Christians in the area said they faced intimidation and discrimination, while Hindu groups claimed conversions were altering the social balance in tribal communities. Those tensions had previously flared into violence, including clashes during Christmas celebrations in **December 2007**.

Analysts said the 2008 violence was fueled by a mix of religion, caste, tribal identity, poverty and political mobilization.

## Government Response

The Orissa state government imposed curfews in affected areas and issued orders allowing police to shoot rioters in extreme circumstances. Additional police and paramilitary forces were sent to Kandhamal, and the central government pressed the state to restore order.

Authorities arrested hundreds of people in connection with the violence, though prosecutions later drew criticism from human rights groups, which argued that many perpetrators were never convicted. Several fast-track courts were established to handle riot-related cases.

State police officials said they were investigating both the killing of Saraswati and the retaliatory violence. Maoist involvement in Saraswati’s assassination was later cited by investigators, but that did little to calm anger on the ground in the immediate aftermath.

India’s central government also sent officials to assess the situation, while the National Human Rights Commission and civil society groups raised concerns about the adequacy of protection for displaced Christians.

## Lingering Impact

Years after the violence, many survivors said they were afraid to return to their villages. Some families rebuilt homes and churches, while others remained displaced or migrated elsewhere.

The riots remain one of the most serious outbreaks of anti-Christian violence in modern India. They drew international concern from church organizations, rights groups and foreign governments, and they continue to be cited in discussions about religious freedom and communal violence in India.

Police and government officials have maintained that they took steps to restore order and prosecute offenders, but victims’ advocates say justice has been incomplete.

For many in Kandhamal, the events of 2008 left scars that went far beyond the official casualty figures — reshaping communities, deepening mistrust and raising enduring questions about the state’s ability to protect religious minorities during communal unrest.

The unrest began in Odisha’s Kandhamal region, a forested and economically poor district with a history of tension between Hindu nationalist groups and Christian communities, many of them from tribal and Dalit backgrounds. Local officials reported multiple deaths and said thousands of people had fled their homes, taking shelter in relief camps, churches, or nearby forests.

Violence has since been reported beyond Odisha, including in the southern state of Karnataka, where churches and Christian prayer halls were attacked in several towns. Police in Karnataka said they had increased patrols and detained suspects after incidents of vandalism and clashes. Christian leaders there accused extremist groups of using the Odisha killing as a pretext to intimidate minority communities.

India’s central government has called for calm and urged state authorities to protect all citizens. Human rights groups warned that retaliatory violence could escalate unless police act swiftly and impartially.

The killing of the Hindu leader has inflamed long-running disputes over religious conversion, caste identity, land, and political influence. Hindu nationalist organizations have frequently accused Christian missionaries of converting poor Hindus through inducements, a charge Christian institutions reject, saying their work focuses on education, health care, and social services. Christian leaders say many converts come from marginalized communities seeking dignity and escape from caste discrimination.

Odisha’s Kandhamal district has seen repeated Hindu-Christian clashes in past decades. Tensions often rise during festivals, conversion ceremonies, or political campaigns, and have been sharpened by competing claims over tribal identity and access to affirmative-action benefits.

Christians make up a small minority of India’s population, while Hindus constitute the overwhelming majority. India’s constitution guarantees freedom of religion, but several states have passed anti-conversion laws, which critics say are used to harass pastors and minority communities.

International observers and church organizations have expressed concern over the latest violence, calling on Indian authorities to investigate both the murder and the reprisals. Officials said additional police and paramilitary forces were being sent to affected areas to prevent further attacks.

“The priority is to restore peace and ensure justice,” one senior official said. “No one will be allowed to take the law into their own hands.”

**NEW DELHI, India (CNN) —** Communal unrest in eastern India’s Orissa state has intensified after mobs attacked Christian neighborhoods in Kandhamal district and set fire to a police station, prompting authorities to impose curfews, deploy additional security forces and arrest dozens of people, officials said.

The violence in Kandhamal, a hilly and largely rural district with a history of tension between Hindu and Christian communities, erupted after local disputes and retaliatory attacks spiraled into broader clashes, police and state officials said. Several villages have reported arson, vandalism and attacks on homes and places of worship, leaving residents fearful and many families sheltering in relief camps or government buildings.

Authorities said a police station in the district was burned by a crowd during the unrest, underscoring the scale of the challenge facing security forces. Additional paramilitary units have been sent to the area, and curfews have been imposed in several towns and villages to prevent further gatherings.

“We are taking all necessary steps to restore order,” a senior state official said. “Those responsible for violence, arson or intimidation will be arrested and prosecuted.”

Police said they have detained numerous suspects in connection with attacks on homes, churches and public property. Officials did not immediately provide a full tally of casualties or damage, citing continuing assessments in remote areas where communications remain difficult.

Christian leaders in Orissa said several Christian-majority neighborhoods had been targeted, with residents fleeing after homes were looted or burned. Some described mobs moving from village to village, forcing families to abandon their homes. Local church representatives have appealed for stronger protection and faster relief for displaced residents.

Hindu organizations in the region have accused authorities of failing to address long-running grievances, while also denying involvement in organized attacks. State officials said they were investigating whether the violence was spontaneous or coordinated.

The unrest has raised fears that tensions could spread beyond Kandhamal into neighboring districts and southward into other parts of India where communal relations are already strained. Security agencies in nearby states have been placed on alert, and political leaders have appealed for calm.

India’s federal government has asked Orissa’s state administration for a detailed report and urged strict action against those involved in communal violence. Human rights groups have also called for an independent investigation, saying previous outbreaks of sectarian violence in the region were not adequately addressed.

Kandhamal has seen repeated friction over religion, land rights and social identity, particularly involving tribal communities, lower-caste groups and religious minorities. Analysts say the district’s poverty, difficult terrain and weak policing have contributed to cycles of rumor, retaliation and mob violence.

For now, residents remain under curfew in several areas, with shops shuttered, roads blocked and security personnel patrolling tense streets. Officials said the immediate priority is to prevent further attacks, reopen relief routes and reassure frightened communities that they can return home safely.
